action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 18/30 and MoCA 13/30 with an amnestic multi-domain profile and no cue benefit; wife documents 8 months of decline (MMSE 22 to 18 in 2 months); no myoclonus; instrumental independence lost: dementia of moderate severity with a rapid course
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: A rapid decline referred as possible CJD needs its tempo, its profile and the absence or presence of prion signs documented at the bedside before any test is interpreted [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic multi-domain profile with near-absent delayed recall and near-chance recognition (storage deficit), impaired naming, fluency, executive and visuoconstructive function
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile, quantify severity, and establish a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Normed testing shows a storage-type amnestic syndrome typical of Alzheimer disease and gives a baseline against which the tempo can be measured [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No hypothyroidism, renal, hepatic, electrolyte or inflammatory derangement; B12 298 pg/mL (low-normal on metformin); glucose 122 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.6% from known diabetes, insufficient to explain the decline
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Metabolic, endocrine and inflammatory causes of rapid decline must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylmalonic acid 0.24 umol/L, normal: no functional deficiency
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to clarify the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A B12 of 298 pg/mL is indeterminate in a man on metformin for 9 years with reduced vibration sense; methylmalonic acid shows whether there is tissue deficiency to treat [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral hippocampal atrophy (MTA 2-3) with temporoparietal and posterior cingulate volume loss; no cortical ribboning, no basal ganglia or thalamic restricted diffusion, no cortical or striatal FLAIR hyperintensity
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia protocol including DWI/ADC sequences to assess for cortical ribboning or basal-ganglia restriction (CJD pattern), medial temporal atrophy, and vascular or structural disease
action_criteria.rationale: DWI is the most sensitive test for sporadic CJD, so the MRI both shows the Alzheimer-type atrophy pattern and answers the referral question [CJD_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced Abeta42 and Abeta42/40 ratio with elevated p-tau181 and total tau; 14-3-3 negative; RT-QuIC negative; no pleocytosis
action_criteria.label: Obtain CSF Alzheimer biomarkers with RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 because the rapid course raises a separate prion-disease question
action_criteria.rationale: The rapid course raises prion disease as well as Alzheimer disease, and one lumbar puncture answers both with RT-QuIC and the Alzheimer biomarkers [CJD_2021] [NIA_AA_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Diffuse slowing without periodic sharp-wave complexes or seizures
action_criteria.label: Obtain a routine EEG because CJD is an active differential in this rapidly progressive presentation; this is not routine Alzheimer testing
action_criteria.rationale: Periodic sharp-wave complexes support sporadic CJD and their absence is reassuring, although EEG is less sensitive than DWI and RT-QuIC [CJD_2021].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not label the diagnosis as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease based solely on the rapid tempo of cognitive decline without confirmation by RT-QuIC, DWI, or EEG
Do not stop the Alzheimer disease biomarker work-up because the decline is rapid; rapidly progressive Alzheimer disease is a recognised phenotype
Do not add an antimuscarinic (oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin) for urinary symptoms; tamsulosin is an alpha-1 blocker, not an anticholinergic, and can continue
Do not attribute the cognitive decline to diabetes; HbA1c 7.6% is a risk modifier that cannot explain a rapidly progressive amnestic dementia
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from his wife documenting the tempo of decline and asking specifically about myoclonus, seizures, visual symptoms, sleep and behaviour

Arrange early review (within about 3 months) to re-measure the tempo and re-examine for myoclonus, pyramidal, extrapyramidal or cerebellar signs; if decline continues at this rate or new signs appear, repeat MRI with DWI and test serum and CSF neural antibodies [CJD_2021].

Offer a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse (72 bpm), conduction history and current medicines; because the dementia is already of moderate severity (MMSE 18/30), consider adding memantine [NICE_NG97].

Keep HbA1c below about 8.0% while avoiding hypoglycaemia, which is the appropriate target for an older adult with dementia; do not intensify with hypoglycaemia-prone agents, and check B12 periodically on metformin [ADA_older_adults_2026].
Assess safety: he no longer drives; review medication supervision, kitchen and home safety, and caregiver support for his wife
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis with the patient and his wife, including a faster trajectory than typical Alzheimer disease, and begin advance care planning while he can take part

avoided_actions.rationale: No cardiac symptom, syncope or QT-prolonging co-medication; an ECG does not answer the rapid-dementia question
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this rapidly progressive cognitive presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
MRI with DWI is available and is far more sensitive for both the atrophy pattern and prion-type change; CT adds nothing
DaTscan evaluates dopaminergic system integrity for parkinsonism; no parkinsonism, tremor, or DLB features are present in this case

differential.key_features: Rapid tempo prompted the referral, but there is no myoclonus, no periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, no cortical ribboning or basal ganglia restriction on DWI, and CSF 14-3-3 and RT-QuIC are negative with an Alzheimer biomarker profile

A subacute amnestic syndrome can be autoimmune, but there are no seizures or faciobrachial dystonic seizures, sodium is normal, CSF has no pleocytosis, MRI shows no mesial temporal FLAIR signal, and the CSF shows an Alzheimer profile; antibody testing is reserved for continued rapid decline
No known malignancy, weight loss or systemic symptoms, and no inflammatory CSF

differential.diagnosis: Frontotemporal dementia (behavioral variant or semantic variant)
differential.key_features: Apathy and mild go/no-go errors occur, but the profile is amnestic with hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy and an Alzheimer CSF profile; no disinhibition or semantic loss

differential.diagnosis: Vascular or toxic-metabolic rapid cognitive decline
differential.key_features: Diabetes and hypertension are vascular risk factors, but DWI shows no infarcts, white matter change is Fazekas 1, and the metabolic panel and MMA are normal
He is flat and withdrawn with GDS 5/15, but denies low mood, and a storage-type amnestic deficit with MMSE falling 4 points in 2 months is not depressive

key_clinical_evidence: Rapidly progressive Alzheimer disease is a recognised phenotype in which decline to dementia takes months rather than years; the tempo that prompts a CJD referral does not by itself exclude Alzheimer disease
The CJD hallmarks are absent here: no myoclonus, no periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, no cortical ribboning or deep grey matter restriction on DWI, and negative CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 [CJD_2021]
Reduced CSF Abeta42/40 with elevated p-tau181 is an Alzheimer biomarker profile; total tau is raised in both conditions and does not separate them on its own [NIA_AA_2018]
A storage-type amnestic deficit with hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy is the clinical and imaging signature of Alzheimer disease

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Rapid tempo alone cannot distinguish rapidly progressive Alzheimer disease from CJD; the discriminating evidence is the absence of myoclonus, periodic complexes and DWI ribboning, with an Alzheimer CSF profile and negative RT-QuIC
red_herrings.data_point: Rapid cognitive decline over 6-8 months prompting urgent referral to 'exclude CJD' by the primary care physician
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchored on tempo may commit to CJD as the leading diagnosis before systematically assessing CJD-specific hallmarks and AD biomarkers

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Elevated total tau is a non-specific marker of neuronal injury seen in both CJD and Alzheimer disease; with reduced Abeta42/40, elevated p-tau181, negative RT-QuIC and a normal DWI it points to rapidly progressive Alzheimer disease
red_herrings.data_point: Elevated total tau in CSF (612 pg/mL, reference <400 pg/mL)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Markedly elevated total tau may be misread as a prion disease marker supporting CJD, particularly in the context of a rapid course

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect, particularly important in a patient with rapid cognitive decline where an undiagnosed structural lesion is possible
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Rapidly progressive amnestic Alzheimer's disease where the rate of decline has triggered an urgent CJD referral; the agent must systematically assess and exclude CJD hallmarks while confirming AD biomarker positivity
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, brain MRI with DWI, and CSF Alzheimer biomarkers with 14-3-3 and RT-QuIC. Recommended: MMA for a low-normal B12 on metformin. Optional: EEG for periodic complexes in the CJD differential.
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of rpAD as a distinct AD phenotype; distinguishes it from CJD through systematic evaluation of EEG, DWI, and CSF prion markers; illustrates that rapid tempo alone does not mandate a prion diagnosis
key_educational_points: Rapidly progressive Alzheimer disease presents with dementia over months rather than years
CJD is excluded by DWI, CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3, EEG and the absence of myoclonus, not by tempo
Elevated total tau is non-specific; the Abeta42/40 and p-tau profile with negative RT-QuIC is what discriminates
Absent myoclonus, absent periodic complexes and absent DWI ribboning together substantially lower the probability of CJD
metadata.real_seed_note: Case demographics and clinical scenario are loosely modeled on published descriptions of rpAD cohorts presenting with CJD-in-differential workups (e.g., Schmidt et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2011; Geschwind et al., Ann Neurol 2008). A specific PMC case report with CC-BY license of confirmed rpAD with CJD exclusion was not identified at the time of authoring; this case is an authentic de novo rpAD construction following the RP-subtype policy. PMC literature search was performed; no single verifiable CC-BY case report meeting all inclusion criteria (confirmed rpAD, CJD excluded by RT-QuIC, positive AD biomarkers) was found.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Pearson is a 68-year-old right-handed retired chemistry teacher referred urgently to the neurology memory clinic by his primary care physician for evaluation of rapidly progressive cognitive decline. His wife, Ruth, provides the majority of the history. Approximately 8 months ago, Mr. Pearson began forgetting names of colleagues he had known for decades and misplacing personal items daily. His wife initially attributed this to stress and the adjustment to retirement. Over the following 2 months, however, his memory deterioration accelerated markedly. He began forgetting conversations he had had hours earlier, asking the same questions repeatedly within a single sitting, and failing to recognize that he had already eaten a meal an hour before. By 5 months ago, he was unable to follow recipes he had previously made from memory, could not operate the television remote without step-by-step guidance, and became disoriented within the familiar neighborhood where he has lived for 24 years. He stopped driving 4 months ago after twice becoming disoriented on routes he knew well. His wife describes the tempo as 'shockingly fast' — 'within six months he went from forgetting names to not knowing where he was.' She consulted his primary care physician, who found an MMSE of 22 at that visit. Over the subsequent 2 months MMSE declined to 18. His primary care physician, alarmed by the rate of decline, searched the internet, read about Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and made an urgent neurology referral with a letter explicitly requesting 'CJD evaluation.' There have been NO witnessed myoclonic jerks, no seizure-like episodes, no bizarre dreams or acting-out behaviors, and no visual hallucinations at any point. His wife expressly denies any 'jerking movements.' His sleep is reported as unremarkable by his wife. He has not had fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, or any new neurological symptoms suggesting a systemic illness. He has no history of neurosurgical procedures, blood transfusions, or dural exposure. He has not consumed wild game or unusual animal products. He has had no recent international travel. There is no family history of prion disease. His mood has been flat and he has been increasingly withdrawn, but he denies being depressed when directly asked. He remains ambulatory without assistance and maintains continence.

neurological_exam.additional: No myoclonus. No asterixis. No alien limb phenomenon. No paratonic rigidity. Go/no-go testing: 2 of 10 errors (mildly impaired inhibitory control). Frontal release signs: bilateral palmomental reflexes present; no snout reflex; grasp reflex absent.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. No dysdiadochokinesia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact and conjugate; no nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Facial movement symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline, no fasciculations. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait mildly uncertain but no frank ataxia. Romberg negative. No postural instability on gentle pull-test. No shuffling, freezing, or festination.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person; oriented to city but cannot identify the hospital by name. States the year correctly but cannot identify the month or date. MMSE 18/30 — lost 4 points on orientation (month, date, building, floor), 3 points on recall (0/3 words at 5 minutes, 0 with category cues), 3 on serial sevens (stops after two correct subtractions), 1 on sentence repetition, 1 on writing (produces a single fragmented phrase). MoCA 13/30 with severe deficits in delayed recall (0/5, 0 recovered with category cues), trail-making (errors on alternating sequence), visuospatial (clock drawing — numbers spaced asymmetrically, hands placed incorrectly), abstraction (0/2), and naming (misnames 'rhinoceros' and hesitates on 'lion'). Verbal fluency: 6 animals in 60 seconds; 4 F-words in 60 seconds. His wife describes the decline as occurring over the past 6-8 months and notes 'he went from not quite himself to needing help with the remote control in just a few months.' No paranoid ideation or formed hallucinations reported.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal muscle bulk. Tone normal throughout — no cogwheel rigidity, no lead-pipe rigidity. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor at rest or with action. No myoclonus elicited by startle, arm extension, or percussion of wrists.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis bilaterally. 2+ patellar bilaterally. 1+ Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Mild bilateral palmomental reflexes present. No grasp reflex elicited.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and temperature sensation intact throughout all extremities. Vibration sense reduced at the bilateral great toes but intact at the ankles. Proprioception intact. No cortical sensory deficits tested (graphesthesia, stereognosis not formally assessed but informal bedside testing intact).
